description:
We are a student-led research and engineering team from New Millennium School, Bahrain, building scientific tools for real mission decisions. For NASA Space Apps 2026, we created RESOLVE, a lunar visibility decision-convergence audit using NASA terrain data, SPICE geometry, reproducible analysis and interactive visualization. We believe the strongest models do more than give answers: they reveal when those answers deserve to be trusted.

We don’t chase certainty. We interrogate it.
summary:
Robustness Evaluation of South-Polar Observation and Lunar Visibility Estimates (RESOLVE) is a lunar landing decision-audit framework built for the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge. It combines a site-and-date navigator with a second question most tools do not ask: does the modeled answer remain stable when defensible modeling choices change?

At candidate site dGR101, the same fixed absolute observer yields a 7.40-day complete simultaneous Sun/Earth geometric-visibility window with NASA Product 78 5 m terrain and 12.92 days with NASA Product 90 native 80 m terrain, a +5.53 -day representation response. RESOLVE exposes that sensitivity, traces it to the modeled horizon, compares observer/reporting assumptions, and links every displayed result to its evidence.

The research itself changed direction: an initial terrain-uncertainty hypothesis was not supported, so we followed the evidence to model sensitivity and then tested it against native NASA terrain products. RESOLVE does not rank terrain products as truth or certify mission safety. Its goal is to make decision stability visible before a precise lunar planning number is trusted.
details:
RESOLVE is a research-first lunar visibility navigator and decision-convergence auditor for the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge. The Navigator lets users explore three supported de Gerlache candidate sites across stored UTC snapshots and inspect whether the modeled centers of the Sun and Earth are above the local terrain horizon. The Audit then asks a second question: if we change a defensible modeling choice, does the planning conclusion stay stable?

Our flagship result is at dGR101. Under the same fixed absolute observer convention, NASA PGDA Product 78 SL2 5 m terrain yields a 7.397830-day complete simultaneous Sun/Earth geometric-visibility window, while NASA Product 90 native 80 m terrain yields 12.923283 days, a +5.53-day representation response. RESOLVE exposes this as MODEL-SENSITIVE rather than hiding it behind one precise number. Users can trace the difference to stored horizon geometry, compare observer and reporting conventions, inspect factor comparisons, and open the exact evidence records behind each claim.

The scientific process is part of the product. R-01A tested an initial terrain-uncertainty hypothesis at dGR203; the limited five-clone pilot did not support it. R-01B changed the research question after a different source of model sensitivity emerged. R-01C then tested that response using native NASA terrain products. We retained the negative result and unresolved limitations instead of tuning the project around a predetermined conclusion.

RESOLVE uses NASA PGDA Products 78, 90 and 104 for south-polar terrain representations, NASA/JPL NAIF SPICE with DE421/MOON_ME_DE421 for geometric Sun/Earth calculations, and published candidate-site literature. The product distinguishes terrain representation, observer convention, temporal sampling, visibility semantics and reporting-domain effects. It does not designate any terrain product as ground truth, claim fine-grid convergence, predict mission success, calculate a communications link budget, or certify landing safety.

The public interface is built with Next.js, React and TypeScript as a static export. Scientific processing and evidence preparation use Python and SPICE-based workflows. A regional 3D terrain context scene was prepared in Blender from the retained NASA Product 90 native 80 m raster, without invented terrain, displacement noise or vertical exaggeration; the physical near-field mechanism remains in the frozen cross-section/horizon evidence rather than the regional 3D view. The site also includes custom SVG/WebGL visualization, a guided demonstration, downloadable evidence and a three-page technical research note. GitHub and Vercel provide public source and hosting, while Playwright/browser and accessibility checks were used for quality assurance.

The intended impact is methodological as much as visual: mission-planning interfaces should show not only a modeled answer, but whether that answer survives reasonable modeling choices. RESOLVE turns that principle into an inspectable workflow: Navigate → Audit → Explain → Evidence. This was done so that planners, researchers, educators and the public can see when a precise answer is stable, sensitive or still inconclusive.
